Introduction

[
1
]

The parties to this family law proceeding,
Euriphile Joseph and Omar Washington, are the parents of two children, Ezekiel
(“Zeke”), born November 1, 2012, and Seraphina, born June 13, 2015.  Mr.
Washington and the children are dual Canadian/U.S. citizens.  Ms. Joseph is a
U.S. citizen and she has permanent resident status in Canada.

[
2
]

Ms. Joseph and Mr. Washington were married on
June 25, 2011 in New York State.  They lived in Brooklyn for about four and a
half years until August 2017, when they and the children travelled to Costa
Rica for what was intended to be a one year “sabbatical” before moving to
Canada.  The sabbatical was extended by almost a year.  They moved to Victoria,
British Columbia in May 2019 and have resided there since.

[
3
]

The parties separated in the summer of 2020.
Ms. Joseph commenced this proceeding in December 2020, seeking an order
permitting her to relocate the children to Brooklyn, and associated orders
respecting the children.  Mr. Washington opposes the relocation of the
children. In addition, he filed a counterclaim seeking a divorce and orders for
shared parenting of the children, child support, spousal support, and property
division, with the most valuable asset being real property in Brooklyn which is
the parties’ former family home.  The most significant issues are whether to
permit the relocation and whether to decline to make orders for property
division on the ground that it is more appropriate for the property division
issues to be determined in New York.

[
4
]

The trial was conducted over nine days between
July 20, 2021 and August 13, 2021.  On August 13, 2021, I reserved my
decision.  On September 3, 2021, counsel for Mr. Washington advised that he
wished to reopen to tender new evidence; specifically, that
he had accepted a new full-time employment position in Victoria.  On September 9, 2021, counsel for both parties submitted a joint
letter confirming their agreement to the admission of this new evidence by way
of an affidavit from Mr. Washington.  On September 16, 2021, Mr. Washington’s
affidavit was filed.  Ms. Joseph chose not to cross-examine Mr. Washington on
the affidavit.  Each party then provided written submissions addressing the
impact of the new evidence on the issues.   With the consent of both parties, I
have considered the new evidence and submissions in reaching my decision.

Background

[
5
]

Ms. Joseph was born in Haiti in 1978.  She is
Black, of African-Caribbean descent.  When she was eight years old, she and her
younger brother moved to New York to reunite with their parents who had
emigrated from Haiti five years earlier. In the meantime, a second son, Jaky
Joseph, had been born to her parents.

[
6
]

When Ms. Joseph joined her parents in New York,
the family lived in a one bedroom apartment in the Bronx. Sometimes her half
siblings, her father’s children from a previous relationship, lived with them.
A few years later, the family moved into public housing in Harlem.

[
7
]

Ms. Joseph’s parents were Seventh Day
Adventists.  She had a strict upbringing and difficult childhood marked by
financial insecurity and what she considered to be emotional and physical abuse
by her mother.

[
8
]

Ms. Joseph attended college in Massachusetts,
graduating in 2001 with a bachelor’s degree in philosophy and political
science. She moved back to New York temporarily and then went to Tufts
University in Massachusetts for graduate school. In 2004, she completed a
master’s degree in philosophy. She returned to New York City where she worked
in a variety of research, policy development and management positions, mostly
for non-profit organizations.

[
9
]

The older of Ms. Joseph’s brothers died in
1999.  Ms. Joseph has a close relationship with her other brother, Jaky Joseph,
who is now 37 years old and lives in Manhattan. Ms. Joseph’s father passed away
in 2007. Her mother still lives in Manhattan, but Ms. Joseph does not have a
relationship with her. Ms. Joseph maintains a close relationship with a half
sister and a cousin who live in Pennsylvania.

[
10
]

Mr. Washington was born in San Francisco in 1972.  His father is
Black, of African-American descent.  His father’s family were Quakers.  His
mother is white, of Jewish heritage.

[
11
]

During the first years of his life, Mr. Washington’s family lived in
California.  They moved to a Quaker community in the Kootenays in British
Columbia when he was about five years old. His sister was born there. The
family moved to Alberta. His parents separated when he was about ten years
old.  He then lived with his mother in Calgary, where he completed high school.

[
12
]

Mr. Washington attended university in Ottawa for one year and then
transferred to the University of British Columbia, earning a Bachelor of Arts
in English Literature in 1995. He later studied jazz and took courses in audio
engineering. He has a strong interest in writing and recording music.  After
university, Mr. Washington returned to the United States where he worked in a
variety of positions including teaching assistant, substitute teacher,
bartender, and DVD technician. From 2006 to 2017, he worked in New York City
for HBO, first as a coordinator in production and then in a management
position.

[
13
]

Mr. Washington’s mother, Susie Washington-Smyth, lives in British
Columbia, on Saturna Island.  He has a close relationship with her although it
is volatile and has been strained at times. His father lives in Calgary. His
sister is an obstetrician who has recently taken a position with Stony Brook
University in New York, which requires her to spend most of each year in
Mozambique.

[
14
]

Ms. Joseph and Mr. Washington met through a mutual friend in
November 2008. They got engaged in February 2010 and began living together in
the summer of 2010, briefly in Brooklyn and then in Harlem.  As mentioned, they
were married on June 25, 2011.

[
15
]

Ms. Joseph and Mr. Washington bought a home in Brooklyn in 2012,
which they still own.  Title was and still is held jointly.  Ms.
Washington-Smyth contributed $25,000 USD to the purchase of the home and
$55,000 USD towards renovations. The parties completed the renovations and then
moved into the home when Zeke was a few months old.

[
16
]

The Brooklyn home is in the Bedford-Stuyvesant neighbourhood,
commonly referred to as “Bed-Stuy”.  Bed-Stuy has long been a centre of
African-American culture.  Its population remains predominantly
African-American.  Originally, Bed-Stuy was a working class neighbourhood.  In
recent years, it has undergone a process of gentrification, attracting young,
ethnically diverse families.

[
17
]

The Brooklyn home is a row house-style townhouse with two suites.
The principal suite, consisting of three bedrooms, two bathrooms, and typical
living spaces, is on the upper two floors.  The parties resided in that suite.
The other suite is a one bedroom unit in the basement which they rented to a
tenant.

[
18
]

Ms. Joseph described the family’s neighbourhood in Brooklyn in
idyllic terms.  She and Mr. Washington became part of a supportive and diverse
community of other young families who lived in the area.  They made close
friendships with many of their neighbours.  They participated in social
activities such as block parties, block beautification initiatives, and
pot-luck dinners.  Ms. Joseph became part of a mother’s group with other new
mothers living in the area.  These mothers babysat each others children and
passed down children’s clothing and supplies.  The children in the
neighbourhood played together.  Zeke made several friends.  There were children
close in age to Seraphina, but she was too young to have developed friendships
before the family moved to Costa Rica.

[
19
]

When Zeke was born, Ms. Joseph quit her job. She was off work for
about eight or nine months and then she took a consulting position.  She went
into the office one day per week; otherwise she worked from home while also
caring for Zeke.  On the days she went into the office, Zeke was at daycare.
Mr. Washington was still working for HBO, and he travelled into the city to his
office.

[
20
]

In February 2014, Ms. Joseph took a full-time job as a project
manager for the City of New York, earning $102,000 USD per year.  Mr.
Washington continued to work full time at HBO earning about $90,000 USD per
year.  The parties hired a nanny to care for Zeke when they were at work.

[
21
]

Later in 2014, Ms. Joseph was recruited to fill the position of
Deputy Executive Director for an organization called Leadership Enterprise for
Diverse America (“LEDA”).  Ms. Joseph’s starting salary at LEDA was $98,000 USD
per year and later increased to $105,000 USD.

[
22
]

Ms. Joseph was working at LEDA when Seraphina was born in June 2015.
She took two weeks off work following the birth and then retuned to LEDA full
time, working from home until Seraphina was two months old.  After that, she
took Seraphina into the office with her.  In November 2015, Mr. Washington took
a brief paternity leave from HBO.  In January 2016, the parties hired an
au
pair
to care for Seraphina when they were at work.  Zeke had, by then,
started pre-kindergarten at the Brooklyn Waldorf School.

[
23
]

The Brooklyn Waldorf School is a private school, with a particular
philosophy that both parties favoured.  Ms. Joseph testified that she did not
fully explore public school options for Zeke but, although she was not
“thrilled with” the public schools in their catchment area in Bed-Stuy, there
were public school options. She said they chose the Waldorf School because she
was confident it would provide a nurturing environment.

[
24
]

The tuition fees at the Brooklyn Waldorf School are steep.  The
tuition for Zeke’s first year was about $25,000 USD.  The parties did not
qualify for financial aid but they received a small scholarship.  Ms.
Washington-Smyth assisted with the tuition payments. Zeke went to the Brooklyn
Waldorf School for pre-kindergarten and kindergarten, leaving in June 2017,
when the parties moved to Costa Rica.

[
25
]

The Brooklyn Waldorf School is a short bus ride from the parties’
Brooklyn home.  Mr. Washington usually took Zeke to school on the bus and Ms.
Joseph usually picked him up, also on the bus.

[
26
]

From time to time, commencing as early as 2010, the parties
discussed the possibility of moving to Canada.  By about 2016, the discussions
became more serious.  Mr. Washington was unhappy in his job at HBO.  Both
parties were working full time, which was tiring with two young children.  They
had long commutes to work which limited the time they had with the children.
Mr. Washington said a concern about crime in Brooklyn, especially gun violence,
was a motivating factor.  Ms. Joseph acknowledged that she considered
Canada to be a safer place to live and she appreciated Canadian gun laws, but
she said these were not the driving factors.  Mr. Washington said institutional
racism in the United States was also a factor.  Ms. Joseph said that her
reality, as a dark skinned woman with dark skinned children, is something she
deals with wherever she is, which I took to mean that institutional racism is
something she thinks the family will encounter wherever they live.

[
27
]

Ultimately, the parties decided to take a one year “sabbatical” in
Costa Rica. Ms. Joseph emphasized that the sabbatical was intended to give the
parties time to plan the family’s transition to Canada; specifically, to
develop a plan for securing employment or developing a business to ensure the
family’s financial security in Canada. Initially, both parties intended not to
work while in Costa Rica, which would allow them to spend a lot of time with
the children and would allow Mr. Washington to focus on his music.

[
28
]

The parties quit their jobs in July 2017.  Steps were taken to
ensure the family’s financial security while in Costa Rica. Specifically, Mr.
Washington negotiated a severance payment from HBO and arrangements were made
to rent the upper unit in the Brooklyn home to tenants (the lower unit having
always been rented to a tenant who was intending to stay). The rental income
was anticipated to be more than enough to meet the mortgage payment and other
costs associated with maintaining the Brooklyn home, with the balance to be
applied towards the parties’ living expenses. The parties also refinanced the
Brooklyn home, generating approximately $120,000 USD which they earmarked for
buying a home or starting a business in Canada.

[
29
]

The family moved to Costa Rica in August 2017.  They rented a
furnished home in a small rural community in the mountains.  Zeke started
attending a Quaker school.

[
30
]

Soon after the parties arrived in Costa Rica, they had problems with
the tenants in the upper suite of the Brooklyn home not paying rent.  They had
to retain a lawyer to assist in resolving that situation.  In addition, living
expenses in Costa Rica were higher than anticipated.  Ms. Joseph became
concerned about the parties’ financial security and she decided to look for a
job. Mr. Washington characterizes this as Ms. Joseph unnecessarily changing the
plan. Ms. Joseph acknowledges that she changed the plan but she maintains that
it was reasonable for her to prioritize the financial security of the family.
Ultimately, Ms. Joseph secured the position of Senior Development Officer with
EYElliance, a coalition focussed on improving global access to vision care. Her
starting salary was $84,000 USD per year and later increased to $88,000 USD.
EYElliance is based in New York, but Ms. Joseph was able to work remotely from
Costa Rica.

[
31
]

While living in Costa Rica, the parties continued to share child
care responsibilities.  Initially, Ms. Joseph cared for Seraphina in the
mornings while Zeke was at school and Mr. Washington recorded music.  In the
afternoons, she worked and Mr. Washington provided the child care.  Later, the
parties hired a nanny to care for Seraphina in the mornings while Ms. Joseph
worked and Mr. Washington focussed on his music.  In the afternoons, he cared
for the children while she worked.  As they always had, the parties continued
to share housekeeping responsibilities, with Ms. Joseph doing most of the
cleaning and Mr. Washington doing most of the shopping and cooking.

[
32
]

Part way through the first year in Costa Rica, the parties decided
to extend the sabbatical for a year and delay the move to Canada. Ms. Joseph
testified that this decision was motivated by her increasing concern over Mr.
Washington’s failure to develop a plan to earn income in Canada.  Mr.
Washington said that he and Ms. Joseph have different approaches to
planning and that he needed to be “on the ground” in Canada to develop a
business plan.

[
33
]

Notwithstanding the extension of the sabbatical by a year, the
parties were determined to implement the plan to move to Canada. Initially, Mr.
Washington wanted to move to Montréal. He did not think Victoria was a good fit
for the family.  He said he preferred a rural lifestyle, but that is difficult
to reconcile with his preference for Montréal.  Ms. Joseph preferred Victoria
because of its proximity to Ms. Washington-Smyth on Saturna Island, and she
thought employment opportunities in Montréal would be limited by the fact that neither
she nor Mr. Washington spoke French perfectly.  After visiting Victoria in
December 2018, the decision was made to move there, although Mr. Washington
continued to express reservations about Victoria.

[
34
]

In May 2019, the family arrived in British Columbia. They spent the
summer on Saturna Island with Ms. Washington-Smyth. They moved into a furnished
rental home in Victoria in September 2019, with a one year lease. Mr.
Washington wanted to ship their furniture from Brooklyn to Victoria but Ms.
Joseph was not in favour of doing so. She explained that she felt financially
insecure because Mr. Washington did not appear to be serious about acquiring
either a business or a job.  In the circumstances, she considered it premature
to incur the cost of moving all their belongings.  Mr. Washington disputes the
allegation that he was not serious about getting a job or acquiring a
business.

[
35
]

After settling into the rental home in Victoria, Zeke started school
at École Beausoleil, a public French language school.  This school was chosen
to cultivate the children’s attachment to Ms. Joseph’s Francophone heritage.
Seraphina was enrolled in daycare for the mornings.  Ms. Joseph continued
working remotely for EYElliance and, because he was not employed, Mr.
Washington naturally assumed most of the day-to-day child care duties including
caring for Seraphina in the afternoons. Ms. Joseph continued to be involved in
the care of the children including participating in morning and bedtime
routines, and helping Zeke with homework.

[
36
]

Ms. Joseph began looking for employment in Victoria.  She contacted
several people who she thought might be able to help her find work that aligned
with her experience and skills.  This included representatives at the
University of Victoria, the British Columbia Government, the Victoria Art
Gallery, the Victoria Foundation, the Inter-cultural Association of Greater
Victoria, Islands Trust Conservancy, as well as executive search firms and an
MLA.  She also conducted searches for specific jobs but found that she was not
qualified for those that met her salary expectations.  She ultimately concluded
that the highest salary she could expect in Victoria was about $80,000 CAD.

[
37
]

Mr. Washington explored the possibility of acquiring a business and
applied for a few jobs.  He maintained that he was serious about finding a job
or developing a business, but Ms. Joseph considered his efforts to be minimal.

[
38
]

By late 2019, Ms. Joseph had become very unhappy in the marriage.
She was concerned about and disappointed by Mr. Washington’s failure to secure
a job or develop a plan to generate income.  She testified that she was
continuing to perform most of the housework as well as her full-time job even
though Mr. Washington was not working. Mr. Washington countered that her
dissatisfaction with Victoria put his job search in limbo.

[
39
]

Ms. Washington-Smyth witnessed the unequal division of labour
between the parties.  She advised Ms. Joseph to stop doing Mr. Washington’s
laundry.  Mr. Washington found out about that and became very angry.  In
February 2020, he sent his mother a vitriolic text message in which he accused
her of a long history of violating, dominating, and trampling him; of
conspiring with Ms. Joseph to manipulate and punish him; and of enabling Ms.
Joseph’s passive aggressive style, among other things.

[
40
]

By January 2020, Mr. Washington proposed moving back to New York. He
said he did that to save the marriage, but he also agreed that going back to
New York was always an option and that is why they rented the Brooklyn home
instead of selling it.  Initially, Ms. Joseph was not in favour of moving back,
but she eventually agreed and put her job search in Victoria on hold.  Mr.
Washington took some preliminary steps toward enrolling the children in a
public school in Brooklyn.  He also applied to the Brooklyn Waldorf School for
both children.  The parties made plans for a visit to the Brooklyn Waldorf
School, with the children, in April 2020.  They booked flights to New York for
that purpose.  Then, the COVID 19 pandemic hit.  The trip was cancelled and the
return to New York was postponed.

[
41
]

By the spring of 2020, Ms. Joseph’s job at EYElliance had become
tenuous.  She started applying for jobs in New York and elsewhere.  Mr.
Washington’s job search intensified.  He applied for jobs in Montréal and New
York, among other places.

[
42
]

On June 24, 2020, Ms. Joseph accepted a position as Director of
Strategy and Operations with the Tobin Project, a non-profit academic research
organization based in Cambridge, Massachusetts.  The job was to start in August
2020 and, initially, it was anticipated that the family would be back in
Brooklyn by then.  She was told that she could work remotely from Brooklyn in
the short term, but would be expected to move to Boston by the summer of 2021.

[
43
]

When Ms. Joseph accepted the position with the Tobin Project,
Mr. Washington had a job prospect in Montréal. She testified that he was
angry that she had accepted a job based in Boston.  He testified that she
became angry when he asked her if she planned for him and the children to move
to Boston with her.  He suggested taking the children with him to Montréal where
it would be easier for Ms. Joseph to spend time with them from Boston. Ms.
Joseph perceived this as a threat to “take the kids away” from her. She became
extremely distressed and suffered what she characterized as a panic attack.
She told Mr. Washington she wanted a divorce. The parties continued to reside
in the same house, but both of them considered themselves separated as of June
24, 2020.

[
44
]

Around the same time, Ms. Joseph’s relationship with Ms.
Washington-Smyth unravelled.  According to Ms. Joseph, this was because she
took the job with the Tobin Project over Ms. Washington-Smyth’s objections, and
Ms. Washington-Smyth then realized she was serious about returning to the
United States with the children.

[
45
]

During the summer of 2020, the parties attended counselling in an
attempt to reconcile.  With the help of their counsellor, they eventually
agreed to return to New York within six months to a year. They rented another
furnished home in Victoria in the meantime, which they moved into when their
first lease expired in late August 2020.

[
46
]

When it became clear that a move back to Brooklyn by August 2020 was
impractical due to the state of the pandemic in New York at that time, the
Tobin Project agreed that Ms. Joseph could work remotely from Victoria in the
short term.  Initially, she was still expected to move to Boston by the summer
of 2021.  Later, she was told that it would be acceptable for her to relocate
somewhere reasonably close to Boston, in the Northeast of the Untied States,
provided she would travel to the Cambridge office on a regular basis.  Ms.
Joseph testified that the Tobin Project has now agreed to extend the deadline
for her return to the United States pending the resolution of this proceeding.

[
47
]

Ms. Joseph started working for the Tobin Project in August 2020. She
works remotely from Victoria.  Her salary is $100,000 USD per year; the
equivalent of about $125,000 CAD.  The position provides her with health
insurance for the family and other benefits.

[
48
]

By September 2020, Ms. Joseph had given up on the reconciliation
attempt.  The parties continued to reside together in the second Victoria
rental home for financial reasons, but Ms. Joseph was determined to end the
relationship.

[
49
]

The children returned to school at École Beausoleil in September
2020.  Initially Zeke struggled a bit, particularly with the challenge of
learning in French.  The school identified some behavioural issues and provided
him with some counselling.  By the end of the school year, in June 2021, he was
doing very well and Seraphina was thriving.

[
50
]

The parties continued to live together until February 2021, which
was the end of the term of their lease.  By that time, Mr. Washington had
changed his mind about returning to New York.  He said he changed his mind when
it became apparent that they would not be returning to New York as a family. He
said the children were doing well in Victoria and he did not want to worsen the
destabilizing impact on them of the parties’ separation by also subjecting them
to another move.

[
51
]

Mr. Washington’s mother bought a home in Victoria, which Mr.
Washington moved into in mid-February 2021. He pays her rent of $3,400 per month.

[
52
]

Also in February 2021, Mr. Washington got a part-time job in content
marketing with PiQPiQ, an internet publishing company based in San Francisco.
Until very recently he worked remotely from home, 25 to 30 hours a week,
pursuant to a consulting contract, earning about $47,000 CAD per year.

[
53
]

Ms. Joseph moved into short term, furnished rental housing in mid-February
2021, where she stayed until mid July 2021.  She then moved into her current
residence which is another short-term, furnished rental.

[
54
]

Ms. Joseph has continued to work for the Tobin Project.  To maintain
the position, she is required to move to the northeast of the Untied States as
soon as practical and then travel to the Cambridge office regularly, as often
as once a week.

[
55
]

The parties have successfully engaged in shared parenting of the
children since their physical separation in February 2021, on a 4-3-3-4
schedule, pursuant to an interim order of Master Bouck granted on February 2,
2021.  Although each of them has displayed some animosity towards the other,
they have been able to put that aside when dealing with issues concerning the
children.

[
56
]

The Brooklyn home continues to be rented to tenants.  The tenancy
for the upper suite was to end on August 31, 2021.

[
57
]

Ms. Joseph’s plan is to return to New York with the children and
move back into the upper suite of the Brooklyn home.  She is in favour of Mr.
Washington relocating to Brooklyn as well, and the parties continuing to
co-parent the children.  She suggested that they both live in the Brooklyn
home, one in each suite, and co-parent in a “nesting” arrangement, but Mr.
Washington is not in favour of that.

[
58
]

Ms. Joseph’s brother has committed to assisting her financially.
With his help, she wants to purchase Mr. Washington’s interest in the home.
She plans to rejoin the neighbourhood community which will provide her and the
children with a great deal of emotional support.  She is confident she will be
able to do that seamlessly as she has maintained good friendships with many of
the family’s former neighbours.

[
59
]

If the relocation is allowed, Ms. Joseph plans to enrol the children
in the Brooklyn Waldorf School.  She has confirmed that there are spots
available for Zeke and Seraphina there.  The tuition for both of them will be
as much as $70,000 USD per year, which she says she will be able to afford with
her brother’s help.

[
60
]

Ms. Joseph plans to continue to work for the Tobin Project, at least
in the short term.  If regularly commuting to Cambridge becomes impractical,
she is confident she will be able to find comparable employment in New York.

[
61
]

Mr. Washington would prefer to remain in Victoria with the
children.  He is in favour of Ms. Joseph staying in Victoria as well, and the
parties continuing to co-parent the children there.  However, he acknowledged
that he would move back to Brooklyn if the relocation of the children is
permitted.

[
62
]

As mentioned, Mr. Washington recently accepted
a new full-time employment position.  The job is with a company called Music
Tribe Brands CA Ltd. Mr. Washington deposed that he is required to work 40
hours a week, on site at Music Tribe’s office in Victoria, and that his
compensation is $90,000 CAD per year plus benefits. The employment agreement he
signed with Music Tribe, which was attached as an exhibit to his recently filed
affidavit, provides that the position “often requires more than normal working
hours” and that it is subject to a three-month probationary period.

[
63
]

Mr. Washington deposed that his new job “blends [his] business and
project management experience with [his] passion for music, and is a great fit
for a long-term career with excellent growth opportunities”.   However, his
affidavit does not describe the nature of his work at Music Tribe, the nature
of Music Tribe’s business, its organizational structure, or the basis for his
optimism about the opportunities presented by the position.  According to the
employment agreement, the external title for Mr. Washington’s position is
“scrum/project management leader” and the internal job title is “performance
scrum leader”, but the agreement does not shed any further light on the nature
of Music Tribe’s business or Mr. Washington’s duties.

Analytical framework

[
93
]

Under both the
Divorce Act
and the
FLA
, a
determination of whether a parent may relocate children is driven by what is in
the best interests of the children. Both parties submit that, in accordance
with the doctrine of paramountcy, the issue should be determined under the
Divorce
Act
:
T.T. v. S.Z.T.
,
2020 BCSC 1628
at para.
42
.  I agree.

[
94
]

The relocation issue may not be decided independently from the
overall question of the parenting arrangements:
K.W. v. L.H.
,
2018 BCCA
204 at para 111
;
Duggan v. White
,
2019 BCCA 200
at para
53
.

[
95
]

Section 16(2)
of the
Divorce Act

states that in determining
the best interests of a child, the primary consideration is “the child’s
physical, emotional and psychological safety, security and well-being.” As was
recently said by Justice Kirchner in
K.P. v. S.K.
,
2021 BCSC 1426
at
para.
87
, “[t]his is the lens through which all factors in s. 16(3) and those
in s. 16.92(1), which apply specifically to relocations, are to be considered”.

[
96
]

Section 16(3) states:

(3)
In determining the best interests of the child, the court shall
consider all factors related to the circumstances of the child, including

(a)
the child’s needs, given the child’s age and stage of development,
such as the child’s need for stability;

(b)
the nature and strength of the child’s relationship with each
spouse, each of the child’s siblings and grandparents and any other person who
plays an important role in the child’s life;

(c)
each spouse’s willingness to support the development and maintenance
of the child’s relationship with the other spouse;

(d)
the history of care of the child;

(e)
the child’s views and preferences, giving due weight to the child’s
age and maturity, unless they cannot be ascertained;

(f)
the child’s cultural, linguistic, religious and spiritual
upbringing and heritage, including Indigenous upbringing and heritage;

(g)
any plans for the child’s care;

(h)
the ability and willingness of each person in respect of whom the
order would apply to care for and meet the needs of the child;

(i)
the ability and willingness of each person in respect of whom the
order would apply to communicate and cooperate, in particular with one another,
on matters affecting the child;

(j)
any family violence and its impact on, among other things,

(i)
the ability and willingness of any person who engaged in the family
violence to care for and meet the needs of the child, and

(ii)
the appropriateness of making an order that would require persons
in respect of whom the order would apply to cooperate on issues affecting the
child; and

(k)
any
civil or criminal proceeding, order, condition, or measure that is relevant to
the safety, security and well-being of the child.

These factors, though not identical, are
substantially similar to the factors set out in
s. 37(2)
of the
FLA
.

[
97
]

Section 16(6)
of the
Divorce Act
also
requires me to consider what is commonly referred to as the “maximum contact
principle”:

(
6)
In allocating parenting time, the
court shall give effect to the principle that a child should have as much time
with each spouse as is consistent with the best interests of the child.

[
98
]

It is well established that the maximum contact principle is not
absolute and must not overshadow the consideration of the children’s best
interests.  In many, if not most, relocation cases, reduced parenting time for
one parent is the only realistic potential outcome,

and in such
cases the focus must be on the consequences to the child of the reduced
parental interaction that would result from the proposed relocation:
A.D.W.
v. B.J.W.,
2018 BCSC 1179
at para.
50
.

[
99
]

Section 16.92
of the
Divorce Act

specifies
additional considerations that apply to a determination of the children’s best
interests when deciding whether to authorize the relocation of a child:

16.92
(1)
In deciding whether to authorize a relocation of a child of the
marriage, the court shall, in order to determine what is in the best interests
of the child, take into consideration, in addition to the factors referred to
in section 16,

(a)
the reasons for the relocation;

(b)
the impact of the relocation on the child;

(c)
the amount of time spent with the child by each person who has
parenting time or a pending application for a parenting order and the level of
involvement in the child’s life of each of those persons;

(d)
whether the person who intends to relocate the child complied with
any applicable notice requirement under section 16.9, provincial family law
legislation, an order, arbitral award, or agreement;

(e)
the existence of an order, arbitral award, or agreement that
specifies the geographic area in which the child is to reside;

(f)
the reasonableness of the proposal of the person who intends to
relocate the child to vary the exercise of parenting time, decision-making
responsibility or contact, taking into consideration, among other things, the
location of the new place of residence and the travel expenses; and

(g)
whether
each person who has parenting time or decision-making responsibility or a
pending application for a parenting order has complied with their obligations
under family law legislation, an order, arbitral award, or agreement, and the
likelihood of future compliance.

[
100
]

Both the
Divorce Act

and the
FLA

stipulate a factor that may not be considered.
Section 16.92(2)
of the
Divorce
Act
states:

(2)
In deciding whether to authorize a relocation of the child, the
court shall not consider, if the child’s relocation was prohibited, whether the
person who intends to relocate the child would relocate without the child or
not relocate.

The corresponding provisions in the
FLA

are
s. 46(2)
(b) which applies when there is no written agreement or order
respecting parenting arrangements and prohibits consideration of “whether the
guardian who is planning to move would do so without the child”, and
s. 69(7)

which applies when there is a written agreement or order respecting parenting
arrangements and prohibits consideration of “whether a guardian would still
relocate if the child’s relocation were not permitted”.

[
101
]

On behalf of Ms. Joseph it was said that
s. 16.92(2)
of the
Divorce
Act
precludes any consideration of what she would do in the event that she
is not permitted to move the children to New York, but that there is no
prohibition against considering what Mr. Washington would do in the event that
the proposed relocation is permitted. Counsel for Mr. Washington did not argue
otherwise. In her oral submissions, his counsel stated what was obvious from
his testimony:  if the relocation of the children is allowed, Mr. Washington
will return to New York with them.  Neither party made substantive submissions
concerning the proper interpretation of s. 16.92(2).  The difficult question is
whether it prevents me from deciding whether the proposed move is in the
children’s best interests by comparing the impact on them of allowing the
relocation against the impact on them of denying the relocation, in a manner
that reflects what I know to be the reality of each party’s intentions.

[
102
]

The Government of Canada website provides the
following explanation for including
s.16.92(2)
in the recent
Divorce Act

amendments:

Parents seeking to relocate with their
children are sometimes required to answer in court the difficult question of
whether or not they would proceed with a relocation if they were not permitted
to bring their children. A response of “I won’t relocate without my child” may
be interpreted as evidence that the proposed relocation is not sufficiently
important and should not be permitted. A response of “I would relocate without
my child” may be interpreted as evidence that the parent is not sufficiently
devoted to the child.

This provision
would prohibit courts from considering this question – or the parent’s response
– if raised in the context of the court proceedings. This will assist in
focusing on the specific legal issue before the court.

[
103
]

From this it appears that the underlying
intention was to ensure there is no presumption in favour of the
status quo

and to prevent unjustified inferences about a parent’s devotion to their child;
in other words, to avoid placing the parent who wants to relocate in what has
been called “a classic double bind”. Those were the concerns identified by the
Alberta Court of Appeal in
Spencer v. Spencer
,
2005 ABCA 262
:

[18] In
conducting this inquiry, it is problematic to rely on representations by the
custodial parent that he or she will not move without the children should the
application to relocate be denied. The effect of such an inquiry places the
parent seeking to relocate in a classic double bind. If the answer is that the
parent is not willing to remain behind with the children, he or she raises the
prospect of being regarded as self interested and discounting the children’s
best interests in favour of his or her own. On the other hand, advising the
court that the parent is prepared to forgo the requested move if unsuccessful,
undermines the submissions in favour of relocation by suggesting that such a
move is not critical to the parent’s well-being or to that of the children. If
a judge mistakenly relies on a parent’s willingness to stay behind “for the
sake of the children,” the status quo becomes an attractive option for a judge
to favour because it avoids the difficult decision the application presents.

[
104
]

However, the application of
s. 16.92(2)
is potentially problematic
because of the way it is worded.  It is clear that it does not prohibit
consideration of the fact that Mr. Washington will move to New York if the
relocation of the children is permitted.  It addresses only what the person who
wants to relocate would do: see
Fotsch
v. Begin
,
2015 BCCA 403
at para.
81
, where
the Court of Appeal makes this point about one of the corresponding provisions
in the
FLA
. It also appears clear that the prohibition applies in all
cases, including cases where the parents have long-standing shared parenting
arrangements and cases, like this one, where the parties are recently
separated, have always shared parenting responsibilities, and the relocation
issue arises on what is, effectively, an initial determination of parenting
arrangements.

[
105
]

If the provision prevents me from considering what Ms. Joseph will actually
do if the relocation of the children is not permitted, then my assessment of
the children’s best interests will be artificially restricted; I will not have
any realistic alternative scenario against which to assess whether a move back
to New York with both parents is in the best interests of the children.  Further,
it would not be possible to appropriately consider the maximum contact principle
without considering what Ms. Joseph would do if the relocation is not
permitted.  It would be absurd to attempt to determine whether the proposed
move, with both parents, is in the children’s best interests without being able
to compare the physical, emotional, and psychological safety, security, and
well-being of the children in that scenario against the physical, emotional,
and psychological safety, security, and well-being of the children in the
circumstances that I know will exist if the relocation is not permitted. Put
another way, it would be perverse to prevent me from considering the options
that actually exist because that would risk an outcome that is not, in fact, in
the best interests of the children.

[
106
]

This problem was noted by the Court of Appeal in
Stav

v.
Stav
,
2012 BCCA 154
at para.
64
, albeit in a case that predated
s.
16.92(2)
of the
Divorce Act
:

I should
observe, however, that I perceive a problem with the stricture against courts
expressly taking into account evidence of what one or the other parent would do
depending on the decision made by the trial judge in relation to mobility. It
is arguable that avoidance of questions giving rise to the double-bind is directed
more to the interests of the parents than it is to the interests of the
children. It may be unfair to place either or both of the parents in the
double-bind, but is it unfair to the children? Is it contrary to their best
interests? Arguably, the answer is that it is only by asking this question of
both parents and assessing their answers, that the court can make a
determination in the children's best interests, cognizant of all of the
options.

[
107
]

Similarly, in
T.K. v.
R.J.H.A.
,
2015 BCCA 8
, a case decided under
the
Divorce
Act

but prior to the
enactment of 16.92(2), the Court of Appeal stated at para. 66:

[66] … Where the
evidence, as in this case, strongly supports a continuation of the pre-existing
joint custody and/or shared residency arrangement as the
only
custodial
arrangement in the best interests of the children, the double-bind questions,
as a matter of practical reality, are relevant considerations to determining
which of only two potential dispositions are open to the judge: shared
parenting in the current locale or shared parenting in the proposed new locale.
In these circumstances, I am of the view that asking both the relocating parent
and the non-relocating parent whether they would move or stay if the relocation
application was granted or refused to be relevant factors, provided that
evidence is carefully weighed together with all of the other relevant
circumstances in determining which of the two potential dispositions could,
practically, be made in the best interests of the children.

[
108
]

In addition, the prohibition against considering
what Ms. Joseph would do if relocation is not permitted when combined with the

the
status quo
which would seem to be unfair to Mr. Washington, who has
always equally shared parenting responsibilities for the children.

,
2014 BCSC 780

s. 69(7)
of the

which, as noted, contains a prohibition similar to
that in
s. 16.92(2)
of the
Divorce Act
.  At paras. 86 to 95, she
observed that before the coming into force of the

, the Court of
Appeal in this province held that it was an error to treat the
status

quo

as a presumption against allowing a relocation, but also that it is necessary,
at least in joint or shared parenting cases, to assess the impact of the

status quo
if the
status quo

is a realistic or viable option (citing
Nunweiler v. Nunweiler
,
2000
BCCA 300
;
S.S.L. v. J.W.W.
,
2010 BCCA 55
;
Stav
; and
R.E.Q. v.
G.J.K.
,
2012 BCCA 146
).   Ultimately, Fleming J. concluded at para. 108,
that s. 69(7) of the
FLA
does not prohibit the court from considering
the
status quo
(see also
A.M.D. v. K.R.J
.,
2015
BCSC 946
at para
52
.).

]

In
Duggan
at para.
18
, in construing
s. 46(2)
(b) of the
FLA
,
Saunders J.A. referred to the double bind as giving rise to a presumption in
favour of the
status quo
that can lead to an incomplete analysis of the
best interests of the child.  At para. 20, she concluded that
s. 46(2)
(b) “is
intended to simplify the analysis and avoid, at least in respect to the
applicant, consideration of what hypothetical circumstances a party may feel
pressured to advance”, and that it directs the court “to the application
presented to the court, for comparison with the respondent’s responsive plans
as presented to the court”.  In that case, the Court of Appeal allowed an
appeal of Ms. Duggan’s failed application to relocate the parties’ son
from the West Kootenay region of this province to the Lower Mainland.  The
Court held, at para. 58, that the trial judge erred by relying on “the
assumption Ms. Duggan would not move without the child” instead of
assessing the actual viable alternatives presented by the parties.  What I take
from this is that s. 46(2) of the
FLA
precludes consideration of
assumptions or hypotheticals.

[
111
]

Whether s. 16.92(2) of the
Divorce Act
can be construed as
bearing the same meaning as
s. 46(2)
and
s. 69(7)
of the
FLA

notwithstanding its somewhat different wording is an interesting question, but
not one that I have to decide.  As I have explained, in this case there is no
doubt about what the actual options are.  If the relocation is permitted, the
parties will co-parent in New York.  If the relocation is not permitted, the
parties will co-parent in Victoria.  Focussing my analysis on which of those
two potential dispositions is in the best interests of the children leads me to
allow the relocation.  In other words, even if I do consider what Ms. Joseph
will do if the relocation is not permitted, I would still find the proposed
relocation to be in the children’s best interests.  In these circumstances, it
is not necessary for me to make definitive findings about the meaning of s.
16.92(2) and, particularly given that neither party made substantive
submissions concerning its meaning, I decline to do so.

Burden

[
112
]

Section 16.93
of the
Divorce Act
stipulates the burdens on a
relocation application, which differ depending on the parenting plan in place.

Section 16.93(1)
states that if the parties “substantially comply with an
order, arbitral award, or agreement that provides that a child of the marriage
spend substantially equal time in the care of each party, the party who intends
to relocate the child has the burden of proving that the relocation would be in
the best interests of the child”. Conversely, s. 16.93(2) states that if the
parties “substantially comply with an order, arbitral award or agreement that
provides that a child of the marriage spend the vast majority of their time in
the care of the party who intends to relocate the child, the party opposing the
relocation has the burden of proving that the relocation would not be in the
best interests of the child”.

[
113
]

Section 16.94
of the
Divorce Act
makes clear that an interim
order qualifies as an order for purposes of
s. 16.93
by explicitly providing
the court with the discretion not to apply the burdens contemplated by

ss.16.93(1)
and (2) “if the order referred to in those subsections is an
interim order”.

[
114
]

In this case, an interim order was granted providing for equal,
shared parenting.  The parties have complied with that order. Pursuant to
s.
16.93(1)
of the
Divorce Act
, Ms. Joseph would bear the burden of proving
that the relocation is in the best interests of the children unless I exercise
my discretion, under
s. 16.94
, not to apply
s. 16.93(1)
.

[
115
]

For reasons similar to those expressed in
K.W.
at paras.
74-94, I have decided to exercise my discretion not to apply
s. 16.93(1)
.

[
116
]

Although
K.W.
concerned the
FLA
, the question in that
case was an analogous one; specifically, whether an interim order qualifies as
an order that would place a relocation application into Division 2 the
FLA

rather than Division 6, the latter of which assumes that an existing agreement
or order has been made in the best interests of the children such that
deference should be given to that pre-established arrangement. The Court held
that when an initial application is brought for an order respecting parenting
arrangements and the applicant indicates in his or her pleadings or by written
notice an intention to change the child’s residence, a subsequent interim order
does not change the fundamental nature of the claim; it remains a claim for an
initial determination of the parenting arrangements that will best serve the
children’s interests.  In those circumstances deference to the interim order is
not warranted.

[
117
]

In this case, Ms. Joseph’s desire to relocate the children is what
prompted the commencement of the proceeding.  The interim order was granted
after Mr. Washington knew that the primary issue was the relocation.
Clearly, the interim order was intended to apply pending the determination of
that issue and following a full assessment of the children’s best interests at
trial.  The interim order did not reflect any consideration of the fundamental
question: in which location should the children reside?  In these circumstances,
it would not be appropriate to place the burden on Ms. Joseph.

The s. 16(3) factors

[
118
]

I will now address the s. 16(3) factors. Those expressed in ss.
16(3)(j) and (k) pertaining to family violence and other proceedings are not
engaged. As noted, although Ms. Joseph testified about what she considered to
be disproportionate displays of anger by Mr. Washington, she also acknowledged
through her counsel that this behaviour did not rise to the level of family
violence, and from her evidence as a whole it is clear that she does not
believe the anger has a material impact on Mr. Washington’s relationship with
the children, his ability to care for them and meet their needs, or the
parties’ ability to effectively co-parent.

The
children’s needs

[
119
]

The first factor expressed in s. 16(3) is “the child’s needs, given
the child’s age and stage of development, such as the child’s need for
stability”.

[
120
]

Zeke is now eight years old. Seraphina is six years old. By all
accounts they are happy, loving, well-adjusted children. Each of them has a
variety of interests and is engaged in a variety of extracurricular activities.
They are both doing well at school. Each of them has made a few friends in
Victoria. They also have some friends on Saturna Island.  They have close,
loving, positive relationships with each of their parents.

[
121
]

On behalf of Mr. Washington, it is submitted that the children’s
needs weigh against the move to New York because they are thriving in Victoria,
he now has the financial ability to provide for them in Victoria even without
support from Ms. Joseph, and Ms. Joseph’s plans for life in New York are
uncertain and speculative. He says that neither party has an employment
position in New York.  He emphasizes that while New York is home for Ms.
Joseph, it cannot be characterized as home for Zeke and Seraphina who were aged
four and two, respectively, when the family moved to Costa Rica.

[
122
]

On behalf of Ms. Joseph, it is submitted that this factor weighs in
favour of the move to New York. She concedes that the children are doing well
in Victoria but she emphasizes that the whole family has deep roots in New
York.  New York is where she has lived most of her life and it is the place
that Mr. Washington lived the longest.  She says that although the children have
made some friends in Victoria, they have not established deep roots there.  She
emphasizes that Mr. Washington was unable to find a job in Victoria for two
years, there is no certainty that he will be able to maintain his new positon
with Music Tribe beyond the three month probationary period, and he has
provided no evidence concerning his plan for caring for the children in
Victoria while also working full time outside of the home.

[
123
]

There is no doubt that all the children’s basic needs can and would
be met in both Victoria and New York City.  Mr. Washington’s submission that
neither party has a job in New York misses the point.  Ms. Joseph has been
assured by the Tobin Project that she can continue to do her job from New York,
provided she travels regularly to Cambridge.  In any event, given Ms. Joseph’s
long and consistent employment history, and the importance to her of financial
security, I have no doubt the children will be provided for financially
irrespective of where they live.  I also have no doubt that they would develop
friendships and have access to health care, good schools, and all manner of
extra-curricular activities in both locations.  I will discuss the advantages
and disadvantages of each location in more detail below when considering the
impact of the proposed relocation on them.

[
124
]

Of course, a move back to New York will be somewhat destabilizing
for the children in the short term.  They will have to adjust to a
neighbourhood they do not remember and a school that will be unfamiliar to Zeke
and new to Seraphina.  However, this does not weigh heavily against the
relocation because I am confident the children will adapt, as they did when the
family moved to Costa Rica and again when they moved to Victoria.  That they
adjusted so well to those moves is a credit to Ms. Joseph and Mr. Washington
who have always prioritized the children’s needs and no doubt will continue to
do so.  There is nothing in the evidence to suggest that the children will have
any trouble readjusting to life in New York.

[
125
]

Further, I am satisfied that Mr. Washington is not fully committed
to remaining in Victoria long term; the children may have to adjust to another
move even if the relocation is not permitted.  When the parties decided to move
to Canada, Victoria was not Mr. Washington’s first choice.  Prior to accepting
the job with Music Tribe, he applied for jobs based in several North American
cities.  He proposed moving back to New York in late 2019/early 2020, and was
still in favour of doing so until about a year ago.  He indicated in his
testimony that he thinks Victoria is “best right now”.  In contrast, I am
satisfied that if the relocation to New York is permitted it is more likely to
be permanent, given both parties’ connections and familiarity with living there
and the employment opportunities available to them there.

[
126
]

There is an aspect of the children’s needs that in my view weighs in
favour of the move.  The parties’ separation is the primary destabilizing force
for these children, and the family and community support available to them in
New York will, in my view, better ease their transition to life with separated
parents.  There is a large community of people in New York who have
longstanding, close relationships with the family and are ready and willing to
embrace them and offer emotional support to all of them as they make this
transition.  Both of the parties developed strong relationships with several of
their Brooklyn neighbours.  Those relationships persist.  Both parties will be
able to depend on those friends for emotional support and help with caring for
the children. I am also satisfied that, in addition to financial support, Jaky
Joseph will be a source of emotional and practical support for both parties.
Ms. Washington-Smyth is the only person in British Columbia with whom the
parties have a comparable history.  Her relationship with Ms. Joseph is now
very strained.  In addition, from a practical perspective, the distance between
her home on Saturna Island and Victoria will prevent her from assisting the
parties with the children on a regular basis and on short notice.

[
127
]

For these reasons, this factor weighs slightly in favour of allowing
the relocation of the children to New York.

The nature
and strength of the children’s relationships

[
128
]

The next factor is the nature and strength of the children’s
relationship with each party and any other persons who play an important role
in their lives.

[
129
]

Clearly, the most important relationships these children have are

[
130
]

If the relocation is allowed, the parties will co-parent in New

[
131
]

A move to New York is likely to result in a strengthening of the
children’s relationship with Jaky Joseph and other members of Ms. Joseph’s
extended family.

[
132
]

This factor weighs slightly in favour of permitting the

Each
spouse’s willingness to support the development and maintenance of the child’s

[
133
]

Ms. Joseph has demonstrated that she is willing to support the
children’s relationship with Mr. Washington.  In her testimony, she repeatedly

[
134
]

I am somewhat less optimistic about Mr. Washington’s commitment to

[
135
]

Nevertheless, this factor is neutral on the question of the

history of care of the children

[
136

Both of the parties have been intimately involved in the care of the
children although, as is often the case, the responsibility for particular

[
137
]

When the children were infants, Ms. Joseph was more intimately
involved in their physical care.  When the family lived in Brooklyn, both

a nanny or
au pair

When the family was living in Costa Rica, Ms. Joseph was working and

[
139
]

When the family moved to Victoria, Ms. Joseph was working and
Mr. Washington was not. He naturally assumed primary responsibility for

[
140
]

It is clear from the evidence, including email communications

[
141
]

Each of the parties has assumed homemaking duties required to
provide the children with a healthy home environment. Mr. Washington did most

[
142
]

In short, this is a case where, although each party tended to assume
responsibility for particular tasks and Mr. Washington spent more time caring

The views
of the children

[
143
]

The views of the children are to be considered, giving due weight
to their age and maturity, unless those views cannot be ascertained.

[
144
]

Dr. Snell determined that only Zeke was old enough for his views to

[

In my view, these children are too young for their views on the

Cultural,
linguistic, religious and spiritual upbringing, and heritage

[
146
]

The children have a complex racial and cultural heritage.  They are
dual Canadian/American citizens.  They are Haitian-American on their mother’s

[

]

149
]

the children’s care

[
150
]

If the relocation is permitted, Ms. Joseph proposes enrolling the

151
]

and after school childcare, or how the children would be cared for if she has

[
152
]

If the relocation is not permitted, Mr. Washington plans to leave

[
153
]

Mr. Washington did not say much about his plans for the care of the

working full time away from home.  He has not provided any evidence of his

[
154
]

The fact that neither party addressed this factor in much detail is

their ability to do that throughout their
marriage and since their separation
.
In the circumstances, this
factor is neutral on the question of whether to permit the relocation.

The
ability and willingness of each party to care for and meet the needs of the
children

[
155
]

As I have already said, both parties have demonstrated that they are
good parents, and that they are able and willing to care for and meet the needs

willing to meet the children’s needs whether or not the relocation is
permitted.

[
156
]

As with the parties’ plans for the care of the children, this factor

The
ability and willingness of each of the parties to communicate and cooperate on
matters affecting the children

[
157
]

The parties have demonstrated their ability and willingness to
communicate and co-operate on matters affecting the children throughout their

towards Ms. Joseph, they have been able to make joint decisions about the

[
158
]

This factor is also neutral on the question of whether to permit the

communicate and cooperate with the other on matters affecting the children.

The maximum contact principle

[
159
]

Again, both parties are good parents and each of them has a good

of the parties.  This conclusion accords with the views expressed by Dr. Snell

[
160
]

There is some overlap between the
s. 16.92
factors and those listed
in s. 16(3), which I have already addressed. The factors expressed in ss.

agreements specifying the geographic area in which the children are to reside

The
reasons for the relocation

[
161
]

The first factor listed in s. 16.92(1) as a
mandatory consideration in deciding whether to authorize a relocation is the
reasons for the relocation.

[
162
]

In
Duggan
, the Court of Appeal addressed the
role of the reasons for a proposed relocation in the assessment of the

, there is no reason to
think a different approach should apply to a relocation case decided under the
Divorce
Act
.   After quoting from
K.W.
and
Stav
, and adopting the
reasoning of those cases, Justice Saunders summarized at para. 17:

It is amply
clear that a court must consider the reasons for the move:
s. 46(2)
(a).
Moreover, as aptly described in
Stav

and reiterated in
K.W.
, the
standard is the best interests of the child. I do not consider that the lens of
“necessity” is the right one. There is nothing in the
Act
that requires
a judge to put the reasons proffered through the strainer of necessity, and
doing so can divert the judge from the proper focus on the child. Full
consideration of the reasons, on the other hand, should meet at least the
standards of reasonableness and good faith. The absence of either of those
qualities may indicate a carelessness of the child’s interests in maintaining
and establishing relationships beyond those with the relocating parent, and
call into question the benefits to the child invariably said to be available by
the relocation. In contrast, the absence of necessity does not negate the
wisdom of a plan.

[
163
]

Ms. Joseph says that she wants to move back to Brooklyn to provide
greater financial and emotional stability for herself and the children, and to
provide them with access to a community of people who share their racial and
cultural identities.  She says there are better income earning opportunities
available to both parties in New York even if she ultimately gives up her job
with the Tobin Project and notwithstanding Mr. Washington’s new job in
Victoria, and the children would benefit from the increased financial
security.  She also emphasises the enhancement of the children’s stability
through the emotional support she and they will be able to draw on in Brooklyn,
and the greater opportunities in New York to nurture their cultural and racial
identities.

[
164
]

Mr. Washington submits that Ms. Joseph’s stated reasons are about
her interests and not the interests of the children; the claimed benefits are
largely speculative; and her plan depends heavily on the generosity of others.
He says that in obtaining his new employment position with Music Tribe he has
demonstrated that both parties are able to obtain satisfying, well-paying work
in Victoria, reasoning that if he can find a good job in Victoria in consumer
electronics and technology, she can certainly find a good position in
government, quasi-government, or the non-profit sector.

[
165
]

Guided by
Duggan
, I start by finding that Ms. Joseph’s
reasons for proposing to relocate the children are reasonable and that her
proposal is advanced in good faith.  Wanting to provide the children with
greater financial and emotional stability and better opportunities to develop
their cultural and racial identities is eminently reasonable. There is no
suggestion that the proposal is an attempt to interfere with Mr. Washington’s
relationship with the children.  To the contrary, Ms. Joseph proposed that Mr.
Washington move back to New York with her and the children and share the
Brooklyn home in a “nesting” arrangement.

[
166
]

Again, in assessing Ms. Joseph’s reasons for relocation, I must stay
focused on the children’s best interests and not the rights and interests of
the parents.  In
Hellberg v. Netherclift
,
2017 BCCA 363

at para.

82
, quoting from
Karpodinis v. Kantas
,
2006 BCCA 272
at para.
27
, the
Court of Appeal reiterated that a proposed move motivated by financial
considerations may “conduce to the best interests of the child”.  In the same
case at para. 84, citing
S.S.L. v. J.W.W.
,
2010 BCCA 55
at para.
33
, the
Court reiterated that “a parent’s emotional state may also be a relevant factor
in determining the best interests of a child, as a child’s interests are
necessarily intertwined with the welfare of his or her parents”.

[
167
]

At present, Ms. Joseph is earning annual employment income of almost
$125,000 CAD.  Until recently, Mr. Washington was earning annual employment
income of about $47,000 CAD.  He is now earning $90,000 CAD, but in a new
position where he remains under probation.  At the time of the trial, their
combined employment income was about $172,000 CND.  They each also receive rental
income from the tenants of the Brooklyn home, but if they stay in Victoria that
will come to an end because the home will be sold. There is no expert evidence
of the current value of the Brooklyn home.  It was last assessed for tax
purposes at $1.4 million USD.  Mr. Washington expressed the view that it is now
worth as much as $2 million USD.  The mortgage balance is about $680,000 USD.
The parties’ combined equity is therefore between about $720,000 USD and
$1,320,000 USD.  If divided equally, they would each receive between about
$360,000 US and $660,000 USD, which translates, roughly, to between $450,000
and $830,000 CAD.  The sale proceeds might provide them with an income earning
asset but whether that is so is entirely speculative because they may apply the
proceeds towards the purchase of a home.

[
168
]

In their respective F8 Financial Statements, Ms. Joseph estimates
her total annual expenses in Victoria at $115,371.72, including income taxes.
Mr. Washington estimates his at $71,055.60, but without accounting for
income taxes.  Neither of them included any child care expenses which reflects
the fact that they were both working from home.  Prior to Mr. Washington
securing the Music Tribe job, considered collectively they were not breaking
even without the rental income.

[
169
]

Ms. Joseph will have to give up her job at the Tobin Project if she
stays in Victoria and, on the basis of her testimony about her efforts in
Victoria to date, I find that she is unlikely to secure a job in Victoria that
pays more than about $80,000 CAD.  I do not agree that the fact that Mr.
Washington recently found a full-time job in Victoria, after two years of
looking, suggests Ms. Joseph will find a job in Victoria commensurate with her
current position in terms of compensation or professional satisfaction.  Her
experience over the last two years clearly suggests otherwise.  With a before
tax income of about $80,000 CAD, she will not be able to meet her expenses,
even before considering the likelihood that she will require some child care if
she obtains a new job in Victoria.  With his new full-time job, Mr. Washington
will also likely require some child care. His expenses will approach or exceed
his after tax income.

[
170
]

The weight of the evidence suggests that the job prospects for both
parties are better in New York.  This is not speculative.  Mr. Washington
conceded as much at trial. The fact that he has now secured a full-time job in
Victoria, after two years of looking, does not change this.

[
171
]

If Ms. Joseph moves to New York she will probably be able to
continue to work at the Tobin Project because Mr. Washington would also be in
New York sharing parenting responsibilities with her and this would provide her
with the flexibility to travel to Boston for work.  Further, I am satisfied by
her evidence and that of Ms. Bleiberg, that if she had to give up her job with
the Tobin Project, she would be able to secure commensurate employment in New
York.  Ms. Joseph testified that she has been in discussions with LEDA and
there is a possibility of her returning to work there at a salary of about
$150,000 USD per year.

[
172
]

Mr. Washington could have continued to work at PiQPiQ from New
York.  That is no longer an option. Nevertheless, given his many years of
employment in New York, the size of the city in comparison to Victoria, the
nature of his work experience, his concession during the trial that his
prospects were better in New York than in Victoria, and his belated success
securing a full-time job in Victoria, I am satisfied that New York presents him
with better professional opportunities than does Victoria.

[
173
]

If the relocation is allowed, the worst case scenario would have the
parties living on Ms. Joseph’s income of $100,000 USD per year in the short
term, until Mr. Washington found a job.  Given his prospects there, I am
satisfied he would likely find employment with compensation commensurate to his
last job there at HBO. It is likely that within a relatively short time, the
parties would be earning a combined income of about $190,000 USD in contrast to
about $180,000 CAD in Victoria.

[
174
]

Leaving aside the cost of private school, there is no evidence in
the record that would support the conclusion that living expenses in New York
are materially higher than they are in Victoria.  Thus, before considering the
cost of private school in New York, the parties would likely be better off
financially in New York.  However, the cost of private school at $70,000 USD
per year would likely eliminate the New York advantage even with Mr. Joseph’s
help, because he would expect the parties to contribute what they could afford
to the tuition costs.  Accordingly, from a purely financial perspective, the
benefit to the children of relocating to New York is likely to be modest.
Accordingly, in assessing whether the proposed relocation is in the children’s
best interest I give no weight to the parties’ likely financial circumstances
in each location, because those circumstances are likely to be similar.

[
175
]

As already discussed in my consideration of the children’s needs, I
am satisfied that the large community of people in New York who are ready and
willing to embrace the family and offer emotional support to all of them will
enhance the children’s stability.  That support will also improve Ms. Joseph’s
emotional state.  In addition, Ms. Joseph is far more likely to be fulfilled
professionally in New York and that will improve her emotional state.  She is
clearly very unhappy in Victoria and the improvement in her emotional state
will allow her to be a better parent to the children.  The evidentiary record
does not suggest that Mr. Washington himself will be happier or more fulfilled
in Victoria than in New York.  These considerations weigh in favour of the
relocation.

[
176
]

The final reason Ms. Joseph gave for proposing the relocation are
the better opportunities in New York to nurture the children’s racial and
cultural identities.  I have already determined that this weighs heavily in
favour of the relocation.

Impact of
the relocation on the children

[
177
]

The next mandatory factor in s. 16.92(1) is the impact of the
relocation on the children.

[
178
]

As I have already said, in many if not most relocation cases,
reduced parenting time for one parent is a realistic potential outcome.  In
such cases the focus must be on the consequences to the child of the reduced
parental interaction that would result from the proposed relocation.  This is
not such a case because Mr. Washington will move if the children move.

[
179
]

In considering the children’s need for stability, I have already
found that their basic needs can and would be met in both Victoria and New
York.  The relocation would not have a material impact on their financial
security, development of friendships, or access to health care, good schools,
and extra-curricular activities.  It would not be materially destabilizing.  To
the contrary, for the reasons already expressed, it would enhance their
emotional stability.

[
180
]

Mr. Washington acknowledged that the children would be warmly
welcomed back by the neighbourhood community in Brooklyn, but he said they
would face an adjustment to living in a large, dense, urban environment.  That
is true, but it does not weigh heavily against the relocation because, as I
have already said, I am confident the children will adapt, as they did when the
family moved to Costa Rica and again when they moved to Victoria.

[
181
]

Mr. Washington submitted that better access to nature is an
advantage of remaining in Victoria over New York.  The beach is a short drive
away from Mr. Washington’s home in Victoria, hiking trails are close by,
and there is a lake about a half hour drive away.  The children have relatively
easy access to Ms. Washington-Smyth’s home on Saturna Island.  There is a
park across the street from Mr. Washington’s home and there are skate parks and
playgrounds close by.

[
182
]

I accept that it will be easier for the children to access natural
environments in Victoria than in New York.  However, even in New York the
children will have access to nature.  The Brooklyn home has a backyard, there
are parks in New York City, there are playgrounds in Bed-Stuy, there are
beaches accessible from Brooklyn, and the Catskills are a three hour-drive
away.  Further, the children will have better access to museums and the arts in
New York than in Victoria, which offsets at least to some degree the easier
access to nature in Victoria.  These impacts do not, in my view, weigh
significantly in either direction.

[
183
]

Mr. Washington submitted that the children will be exposed to more
racism in New York than in Victoria, and that racism, the prevalence of guns,
and the crime rates in New York weigh against the relocation.  He testified
about some personal experiences with racism in New York and tendered some
statistical evidence about gun violence in Brooklyn.  There is no evidence of
the extent to which these are issues in Victoria.  It might be appropriate for
me to take judicial notice of the fact that there are more privately owned guns
and higher crime rates in New York than in Victoria; however, the record
provides no foundation for making findings about the extent to which racism and
racial profiling are more prevalent in New York.

[
184
]

Without intending to suggest that racism, crime, and gun violence
are not serious problems, it almost goes without saying that countless children
of colour grow up safely and happily in New York City, and go on to live
productive, successful lives.  Ms. Joseph has lived in New York for most of her
life.  As a Black mother of children of colour, she is intimately familiar with
these issues and she believes returning to New York is in the children’s best
interests. As I have already explained, I found Ms. Joseph to be a credible
witness and a devoted mother.  I fully accept that she believes it is in
the children’s best interests for them to return to New York, notwithstanding
the reality of racism, gun violence, and crime, and I respect her assessment of
these issues. Again, for the reasons I have already expressed, I am not as
confident about the veracity of Mr. Washington’s stated belief that it is
better for the children to stay in Victoria.  As late as last
summer, he was in favour of moving back to New York.  This suggests that he has
overstated his own concern about these issues.

[
185
]

On balance, for the reasons I have already expressed, the impact on
the children of a move to New York would be positive.

Time spent
with the children and the level of involvement in their lives

[
186
]

Section 16.92(1)(c) requires me to consider the amount of time spent
with the children by each party and the level of involvement in the children’s
lives of each of the parties. These factors have already been addressed in my
discussion of the history of the children’s care, and the ability and
willingness of the parties to care for and meet their needs.  In summary, each
of the parties has always spent substantial time with the children and has been
intimately involved in their care.  This would not change if the relocation is
permitted.

The
reasonableness of the proposal of the person who intends to relocate the
children to vary the exercise of parenting time, decision-making responsibility,
or contact

[
187
]

The next relevant s. 16.92(1) factor is the reasonableness of the
proposal of the person who intends to relocate the children to vary the
exercise of parenting time, decision-making responsibility, or contact, taking
into consideration, among other things, the location of the new place of
residence and the travel expenses.

[
188
]

Ms. Joseph’s proposal to continue joint decision making and to have
the children spend most of their school vacation time with Mr. Washington was
reasonable given the distance between New York and Victoria.  However, it did
not reflect reality because, as I have said repeatedly, there is no doubt that
the parties will reside in close proximity whether that is in New York or
Victoria.  Ms. Joseph was clear that if Mr. Washington moved to New York, she
would support the continuation of the existing shared parenting regime.

Compliance
with obligations and the likelihood of future compliance

[
189
]

The final mandatory factor is whether each party has complied with their
obligations under family law legislation, any order, award, or agreement, and
the likelihood of future compliance.  Both parties have done so.  I have no
doubt they will continue to do so.

Conclusion on relocation

[
190
]

The children are likely to be financially secure whether they reside
in New York or in Victoria.  They would have the opportunity to develop
friendships and they would have access to health care, good schools, and
extra-curricular activities in both locations.  However, the enhanced emotional
stability and increased opportunities to nurture their racial and cultural
identities that will inure to the children’s benefit if they return to New York
weigh heavily in favour of permitting the relocation.  There is little if any
downside to the proposed move.  The children have not established deep roots in
Victoria.  The move will not be materially destabilizing for them.  Most
importantly, it will not impact on the time they spend with their father or the
quality of their relationship with him.  The most significant disadvantage of
moving is the distance a move will place between the children and Ms.
Washington-Smyth, but she has demonstrated a commitment to maintaining her
relationship with them wherever they live.  The advantages of the relocation
outweigh the disadvantages.

[
191
]

Having considered all the mandatory factors through the lens of the
primary consideration – the children’s physical, emotional, and psychological
safety, security, and well-being – I have no hesitation in concluding that the proposed
relocation to New York is in their best interests.

[
192
]

There is no dispute that at the time he resigned from HBO he was earning about

193
]

Ms. Joseph’s current income gives rise to an obligation to pay

[
194
]

The parties currently have equal parenting time. On the record, I am
