Property division

[
196
]

There is no dispute that, pursuant to
s. 106(2)

of the
FLA
, I have the jurisdiction in this case to make orders
respecting property division.  The question is whether I should decline to do
so.  The governing provisions in the
FLA
are
s. 106(4)
,
(5)
, and

(6)
:

(4) Despite subsection (2), a court may
decline to make an order under this Part if the court, having regard to the
interests of the spouses and the ends of justice, considers that it is more
appropriate for jurisdiction to be exercised outside British Columbia.

(5) In determining whether to decline
jurisdiction under subsection (4), the court must consider all of the
following:

(a) [Repealed
2014-9-15.]

(b) the relative
convenience and expense for the spouses and their witnesses;

(c) if section 108
[
choice of law rules
] applies, the law to be applied to issues in the
proceeding;

(d) the
desirability of avoiding multiple proceedings or conflicting decisions in
different courts or tribunals;

(e) the extent to
which an order respecting property or debt

(i)  made in
another jurisdiction would be enforceable in British Columbia, and

(ii)  made in
British Columbia would be enforceable in another jurisdiction;

(f) the fair and
efficient working of the Canadian legal system as a whole;

(g) any other
circumstances the court considers relevant.

(6) A
determination of authority under subsection (2) or of whether to decline
jurisdiction under subsection (4) is to be made solely by reference to this
section.

[
197
]

All but one of the factors expressed in s. 106(5) weigh in favour of
exercising my discretion in this case. The exception is that in s. 106(5)(c):
“if section 108 applies, the law to be applied to issues in the proceeding”.

[
198
]

In its relevant respects, s. 108 provides that if the parties’ first
common habitual residence during their relationship was in a jurisdiction in which
a “regime of community of property” applies, property owned or acquired and
debt owing or acquired during the relationship that is property or debt to
which the regime of community of property applies must be divided at the end of
the relationship according to that regime of community of property.  This is
mandatory: s. 108(2) and (5).

[
199
]

There is no dispute that the parties’ first common habitual
residence during their relationship was the state of New York and that most if
not all the property and debt in issue was acquired and remains in New York.
There is no dispute that if New York is a jurisdiction in which a regime of
community of property applies, then I am compelled to apply New York law to
most if not all the property issues.  The problem is that there is no evidence
upon which I can determine whether New York is a jurisdiction in which a regime
of community of property applies.

[
200
]

I was provided with excerpts from New York statutory law that
suggest that New York is not a jurisdiction in which a regime of community of
property applies, but that is insufficient.  As recently observed by Justice Veenstra
in
X.W.L. v. J.L
.,
2021 BCSC 860
at para.
10
, foreign law is a question
of fact that must be established by admissible evidence.  To prove New York
law, evidence is required from a properly qualified expert that also complies
with the requirements of Rule 13-2 of the
Supreme Court Family Rules
,
which requires that the person giving the opinion certify that they are aware
of their duties to the court, and that they are not an advocate for either
party.

[
201
]

Again, s. 108 of the
FLA
requires that most if not all of the
property issues in this case be decided under New York law if New York is a
jurisdiction in which a regime of community of property applies.  I am unable
to determine whether New York is a jurisdiction in which a regime of community
of property applies.  In these circumstances, I decline to make orders for
property division because it is more appropriate for jurisdiction to be excised
outside British Columbia.

[
202
]

I appreciate that obtaining admissible evidence from a qualified
lawyer about whether a “regime of community of property” exists in New York
and, if so, whether any of the property in issue is property to which that
regime applies imposes an additional burden and cost on the parties, but there
is no way to avoid it given the clear wording of
s. 108
of the
FLA
.
